iono_cat.label: Ionotropic · cation channel
iono_cat.means: A ligand-gated ion channel. The transmitter itself opens a pore through the receptor, cations rush in and the membrane depolarises. Fast, and over in milliseconds.

iono_cl.label: Ionotropic · chloride channel
iono_cl.means: A ligand-gated ion channel that passes chloride. When the transmitter binds, chloride flows in and the cell is held down or shunted: inhibition, fast and brief.

iglur.label: Ionotropic · glutamate receptor
iglur.means: A tetramer whose four clamshell domains each close on a glutamate; the pore opens for cations. Fast excitation, and the machinery of most synaptic plasticity.

gs.label: Metabotropic · GPCR, Gs
gs.means: A G-protein-coupled receptor: seven helices through the membrane and no pore. Binding changes its shape and switches on a G protein inside. Gs raises cAMP, which turns on protein kinase A. Slower than a channel, and its effects last.

gi.label: Metabotropic · GPCR, Gi/o
gi.means: A G-protein-coupled receptor working through Gi/o: it lowers cAMP, opens K⁺ channels and closes Ca²⁺ channels. The net effect is to quieten the cell or the terminal it sits on.

voltage.means: Not a receptor: nothing binds it. A charged helix in each domain senses the membrane potential and pulls the gate open when the cell depolarises. These are what turn a receptor's small voltage change into an action potential, or let Ca²⁺ in to release transmitter.

leak.label: Background channel
leak.means: A channel open at rest, or gated from inside the cell rather than by a transmitter. These set the resting potential and how easily a cell fires.

cak.means: A potassium channel opened by calcium arriving inside the cell. It follows every burst of activity with a pause, and shapes how fast a neuron can fire.

transporter.means: Not a receptor: a carrier that binds the transmitter and hauls it across a membrane, one molecule per cycle, driven by an ion gradient. Reuptake transporters end the signal; vesicular ones load the next one.

glossary.Ionotropic: A receptor that is itself an ion channel. The transmitter lands on it and the pore opens within a millisecond; ions flow and the membrane potential changes at once. Fast, and finished as soon as the transmitter leaves. The electrical, moment-to-moment side of signalling.
glossary.Metabotropic: A receptor with no pore of its own. When the transmitter binds it switches on a G protein inside the cell, which sets off chemical messengers (cAMP, IP₃, Ca²⁺) that open or close channels and change the cell over seconds to minutes. Slower to start than a channel and lasting far longer: the mood-setting side of signalling.
glossary.GPCR: G-protein-coupled receptor: the commonest kind of receptor in the body, one protein that snakes through the membrane seven times, holding a G protein on the inside. About a third of all medicines act on one. Which G protein it holds, Gs, Gi/o or Gq, decides what it does when bound.
glossary.Gs: The stimulatory G protein. It switches on adenylyl cyclase, so cAMP rises and protein kinase A wakes up. Tends to excite the cell and strengthen its responses.
glossary.Gi/o: The inhibitory G protein. It switches adenylyl cyclase off so cAMP falls, and its βγ arm opens K⁺ channels and closes Ca²⁺ channels. Tends to quieten the cell, or stop a terminal releasing.
glossary.Gq: The G protein that turns on phospholipase C, which splits a membrane lipid into IP₃ and DAG. IP₃ releases Ca²⁺ from the cell's stores and DAG switches on protein kinase C. Usually excitation, with a long tail.
glossary.cation channel: A pore for positive ions: Na⁺ and K⁺, sometimes Ca²⁺. Opening it lets Na⁺ rush in, so the inside of the cell becomes more positive and moves towards the threshold for an action potential. Excitatory.
glossary.chloride channel: A pore for chloride. Opening it lets Cl⁻ in, which holds the membrane at or below its resting potential, so the cell is harder to fire. Inhibitory in the adult brain.
glossary.glutamate receptor: The AMPA, NMDA and kainate receptors: four subunits, each with a clamshell that closes on a glutamate, around a pore for cations. The fast excitatory synapse of the brain, and the machinery of learning.
glossary.Voltage-gated channel: Not a receptor: nothing binds it. A charged helix inside it senses the voltage across the membrane and pulls the gate open when the cell depolarises. Sodium channels make the action potential, potassium channels end it, calcium channels turn it into transmitter release.
glossary.Background channel: A channel open at rest, or opened from inside the cell rather than by a transmitter. These set the resting potential and how easily a neuron fires.
glossary.Ca²⁺-activated K⁺ channel: A potassium channel opened by calcium arriving inside the cell, so every burst of activity is followed by a pause.
glossary.Transporter: Not a receptor: a carrier protein that binds a transmitter and hauls it across the membrane one molecule at a time, powered by the sodium gradient. Reuptake transporters pull transmitter out of the synapse to end the signal, and are what most antidepressants and stimulants block; vesicular transporters load it into vesicles for the next release.
glossary.affinity: How tightly a receptor holds its transmitter: high affinity means it is occupied at low concentrations and lets go slowly, low affinity means it needs a lot and lets go fast. A synapse releases transmitter in a brief burst of very high concentration, so low-affinity receptors like AMPA answer only to release right in front of them, while high-affinity receptors like D2 sense the faint background level too.
glossary.agonist: A molecule that binds a receptor and switches it on, as the transmitter itself does. Morphine is an agonist at the μ-opioid receptor; nicotine at nicotinic receptors.
glossary.antagonist: A molecule that binds a receptor and blocks it, so the transmitter cannot act. Naloxone at the μ-opioid receptor; antipsychotics at D2; antihistamines at H1.
glossary.autoreceptor: A receptor on the terminal that released the transmitter, sensing how much is out there and turning release down. The cell's own volume control.

groups.name: Glutamate receptors
groups.note: The excitatory receptors. Three kinds of channel and eight G-protein-coupled receptors answer to the same transmitter, at different speeds.

items.name: AMPA receptor
items.binds: Glutamate, with low affinity: it needs the millimolar burst a synapse releases, and lets go within a millisecond. AMPA itself is the selective agonist it is named for.
items.drugs: Perampanel (epilepsy) blocks it. Ketamine's antidepressant effect is thought to end here, by boosting AMPA signalling.
items.effect: Opens for Na⁺ and K⁺, depolarising the spine. GluA2-containing receptors exclude Ca²⁺; those without it let Ca²⁺ in.
items.note: The workhorse of fast excitation. Adding and removing AMPA receptors from a spine is what long-term potentiation and depression mostly are.

items.name: NMDA receptor
items.binds: Glutamate at the GluN2 subunits, with high affinity, and glycine or D-serine at GluN1, which must also be occupied. At rest a Mg²⁺ ion plugs the pore.
items.drugs: Ketamine and esketamine (Spravato) block it, as do PCP, nitrous oxide in part, dextromethorphan (cough medicine) and memantine (Alzheimer's). Alcohol dampens it, which is part of both the drunkenness and the blackout.
items.effect: Passes Ca²⁺ as well as Na⁺, but only once the membrane is already depolarised enough to expel the Mg²⁺: a coincidence detector for input and activity.
items.note: The trigger for most synaptic plasticity, and the receptor ketamine, PCP and memantine block.

items.name: Kainate receptor
items.binds: Glutamate, at an affinity between AMPA's and NMDA's; kainate, a seaweed toxin, is its selective agonist.
items.drugs: Topiramate (epilepsy, migraine) blocks it in part. No drug aims at it alone.
items.effect: A slower, smaller cation current than AMPA, on both sides of the synapse: postsynaptic in the hippocampus, presynaptic where it tunes release.
items.note: Less abundant than the other two, and still the least understood.

items.name: mGluR1
items.binds: Glutamate, with high affinity; group I with mGluR5. Sits at the edge of the synapse rather than under it, so it answers to strong or repeated release.
items.drugs: None in everyday use.
items.effect: Gq: IP₃, Ca²⁺ from stores, PKC; a slow excitatory current. In the cerebellum it drives long-term depression at parallel-fibre synapses.
items.note: Concentrated in Purkinje cells and the thalamus.

items.name: mGluR5
items.binds: Glutamate, high affinity; group I. Held at the synapse edge by Homer proteins, coupled to the NMDA receptor.
items.drugs: None approved; mavoglurant and basimglurant were tried for fragile X and depression.
items.effect: Gq signalling, Ca²⁺ oscillations, and a boost to NMDA currents. Drives the protein synthesis behind some long-term depression.
items.note: The receptor over-active in fragile X syndrome; the target of trials there and in addiction.

items.name: mGluR2
items.binds: Glutamate, moderate affinity; group II. Presynaptic, and mostly outside the active zone, so it senses spill-over.
items.drugs: None approved; pomaglumetad was tried as an antipsychotic.
items.effect: Gi/o: lowers cAMP and reduces release from the terminal it sits on. An autoreceptor that turns the volume down.
items.note: Agonists were tried as antipsychotics; the receptor is thick in the prefrontal cortex.

items.name: mGluR3
items.binds: Glutamate; group II, and also on astrocytes, where it senses what the synapse spills.
items.drugs: None in everyday use.
items.effect: Gi/o: damps release and, in glia, sets off the release of growth factors.
items.note: Variants are linked to schizophrenia risk.

items.name: mGluR4
items.binds: Glutamate, low affinity; group III. Presynaptic, in the active zone.
items.drugs: None approved; foliglurax was tried for Parkinson's.
items.effect: Gi/o: cuts release at the terminal. In the basal ganglia it damps the striatopallidal pathway.
items.note: A target under study for Parkinson's disease.

items.name: mGluR6
items.binds: Glutamate; group III. Found on one cell only: the ON bipolar cell of the retina.
items.drugs: None.
items.effect: Gαo closes a cation channel (TRPM1), so the bipolar cell is inhibited by glutamate and depolarises when the photoreceptor stops releasing it in the light.
items.note: The reason there is an ON pathway at all. Mutations cause congenital stationary night blindness.

items.name: mGluR7
items.binds: Glutamate, with the lowest affinity of the family: it needs the concentration right inside the active zone, where it sits.
items.drugs: None in everyday use.
items.effect: Gi/o: a brake on release, engaged only during high-frequency firing.
items.note: The most widespread of the group III receptors.

items.name: mGluR8
items.binds: Glutamate, moderate affinity; group III, presynaptic.
items.drugs: None in everyday use.
items.effect: Gi/o: reduces release, in the hippocampus and the olfactory bulb among others.
items.note: Studied in anxiety and in epilepsy.

groups.name: GABA and glycine receptors
groups.note: The inhibitory receptors: two chloride channels and one G-protein-coupled receptor.

items.name: GABA-A receptor
items.binds: GABA at two sites between the α and β subunits, opening at micromolar GABA. Benzodiazepines bind a separate site at the α–γ interface and make GABA more effective; barbiturates, neurosteroids, alcohol and propofol each have a site of their own.
items.drugs: The benzodiazepines: diazepam (Valium), lorazepam, alprazolam (Xanax), clonazepam. The sleeping pills zolpidem (Ambien) and zopiclone. Barbiturates, propofol and the gas anaesthetics. Alcohol, which potentiates it. Muscimol from the fly agaric mushroom. Brexanolone and zuranolone, the neurosteroid antidepressants.
items.effect: Opens for Cl⁻ within a millisecond. In a mature neuron chloride flows in and hyperpolarises or shunts the cell; in the newborn brain, where chloride is high inside, the same channel excites.
items.note: A pentamer assembled from nineteen possible subunits; the mix decides where it sits and what drugs touch it. α5 in the hippocampus, α6 in cerebellar granule cells, δ-containing receptors outside the synapse for tonic inhibition.

items.name: GABA-A ρ receptor (GABA-C)
items.plain: GABA type A receptor, ρ subunits
items.binds: GABA, with higher affinity than the ordinary GABA-A receptor and much slower to let go. Insensitive to benzodiazepines and to bicuculline.
items.drugs: None; it ignores benzodiazepines.
items.effect: A small, sustained Cl⁻ current.
items.note: Mostly in the retina, on bipolar cell terminals.

items.name: GABA-B receptor
items.binds: GABA, with high affinity, and baclofen. Works only as a pair: GABA-B1 binds, GABA-B2 signals.
items.drugs: Baclofen (spasticity, and used off-label for alcohol dependence). GHB and sodium oxybate (narcolepsy) act here in part.
items.effect: Gi/o: opens GIRK K⁺ channels on the dendrite for a slow, long hyperpolarisation, and closes Ca²⁺ channels on terminals to cut release, of GABA itself included.
items.note: The slow phase of inhibition; baclofen's target in spasticity.

items.name: Glycine receptor
items.binds: Glycine, high affinity, at the interfaces of a pentamer of α and β subunits; also taurine and β-alanine, weakly. Strychnine blocks it.
items.drugs: Strychnine, the rat poison, blocks it. Alcohol and gas anaesthetics potentiate it.
items.effect: Opens for Cl⁻: fast inhibition.
items.note: The chief inhibitory receptor of the spinal cord and brainstem, on motor neurons among others. Mutations cause hyperekplexia, the startle disease.

groups.name: Acetylcholine receptors
groups.note: Two families that share nothing but the transmitter: the nicotinic channels, named for tobacco's alkaloid, and the muscarinic G-protein-coupled receptors, named for a mushroom's.

items.name: Nicotinic, muscle type
items.binds: Two acetylcholines, one at each α1 subunit interface, with micromolar affinity. Curare and α-bungarotoxin block it; the antibodies of myasthenia gravis destroy it.
items.drugs: The muscle relaxants of surgery: rocuronium, vecuronium, succinylcholine. Curare, the arrow poison. Cobra and krait venoms block it; that is what paralyses.
items.effect: A large, fast cation current that depolarises the muscle fibre past threshold every time.
items.note: The receptor at the neuromuscular junction, (α1)₂β1δε in the adult, and the first receptor ever isolated.

items.name: Nicotinic α4β2
items.binds: Acetylcholine and nicotine, both with high affinity: this is the receptor nicotine is addictive through. Varenicline is a partial agonist here.
items.drugs: Nicotine, in cigarettes, vapes and patches. Varenicline (Champix, Chantix) and cytisine, the quitting drugs, are partial agonists here.
items.effect: Cation current, and a rise in Ca²⁺ that boosts transmitter release from the terminals it sits on.
items.note: The commonest nicotinic receptor in the brain, on dopamine neurons of the ventral tegmental area among many others.

items.name: Nicotinic α7
items.binds: Acetylcholine with low affinity and choline as well; α-bungarotoxin blocks it. Desensitises within milliseconds.
items.drugs: Nicotine. Galantamine (Alzheimer's) makes it more responsive. Bupropion blocks it weakly.
items.effect: Unusually permeable to Ca²⁺ for a nicotinic receptor, so it signals like a second messenger as much as a channel.
items.note: A homopentamer, dense in the hippocampus; on microglia it damps inflammation.

items.name: Nicotinic α3β4
items.binds: Acetylcholine, with moderate affinity; the ganglionic receptor, blocked by hexamethonium.
items.drugs: Nicotine. Mecamylamine blocks it; bupropion (Zyban, Wellbutrin) blocks it in part, one reason it helps people stop smoking.
items.effect: Fast cation current.
items.note: Carries every autonomic signal through its ganglion, and sits in the medial habenula, where it shapes nicotine aversion.

items.name: Muscarinic M1
items.binds: Acetylcholine, with high affinity; pirenzepine is the selective antagonist.
items.drugs: Blocked by scopolamine (motion-sickness patches), atropine, and as a side effect by tricyclic antidepressants, old antihistamines and some antipsychotics: the dry mouth and fuzzy memory. Donepezil and rivastigmine raise acetylcholine to reach it.
items.effect: Gq: closes the M-type K⁺ channel and raises Ca²⁺, making the cell more excitable for seconds.
items.note: The main muscarinic receptor of the cortex and hippocampus, and the one behind acetylcholine's part in memory.

items.name: Muscarinic M2
items.binds: Acetylcholine, high affinity; methoctramine blocks it.
items.drugs: Atropine, which speeds the heart by blocking it. Ipratropium and tiotropium inhalers.
items.effect: Gi/o: opens GIRK K⁺ channels and lowers cAMP. On cholinergic terminals it is the autoreceptor that limits release; in the heart it slows the beat.
items.note: The vagus nerve's receptor on the sinoatrial node.

items.name: Muscarinic M3
items.binds: Acetylcholine, high affinity.
items.drugs: Oxybutynin and solifenacin (overactive bladder), tiotropium and ipratropium (COPD inhalers) block it; pilocarpine (dry mouth, glaucoma) switches it on.
items.effect: Gq: Ca²⁺ release, contraction, secretion.
items.note: Smooth muscle and glands: the receptor of salivation, bronchoconstriction and the bladder. Sparse in the brain.

items.name: Muscarinic M4
items.binds: Acetylcholine, high affinity.
items.drugs: Xanomeline, in the 2024 antipsychotic Cobenfy, switches it on: the first antipsychotic that does not touch dopamine receptors.
items.effect: Gi/o: lowers cAMP; on striatal neurons it opposes dopamine's D1 signal.
items.note: Concentrated in the striatum; a target in trials for psychosis.

items.name: Muscarinic M5
items.binds: Acetylcholine, high affinity.
items.drugs: None in everyday use.
items.effect: Gq signalling; on dopamine neurons it prolongs their firing and dopamine release.
items.note: The rarest muscarinic receptor, on the dopamine cells of the midbrain and on cerebral blood vessels.

groups.name: Dopamine receptors
groups.note: Five G-protein-coupled receptors in two families: D1-like raise cAMP, D2-like lower it.

items.name: Dopamine D1
items.binds: Dopamine, with low affinity, so it answers to the burst of release that follows an unexpected reward rather than the steady background level.
items.drugs: No drug in everyday use acts on it directly. Cocaine, amphetamine and methylphenidate reach it by raising dopamine.
items.effect: Gs: raises cAMP, phosphorylating DARPP-32; on striatal direct-pathway neurons it says 'go'.
items.note: The most abundant dopamine receptor, in the striatum, nucleus accumbens and prefrontal cortex.

items.name: Dopamine D2
items.binds: Dopamine, with high affinity, enough to sense the tonic level and to notice when it dips. Every antipsychotic blocks it; the potency of the older ones tracks their D2 affinity exactly.
items.drugs: Every antipsychotic blocks it: haloperidol, risperidone, olanzapine, quetiapine, aripiprazole (a partial agonist). Metoclopramide and domperidone (anti-sickness), which is why they can cause tremor. The Parkinson's drugs pramipexole, ropinirole and rotigotine switch it on, and levodopa reaches it as dopamine. Cabergoline and bromocriptine.
items.effect: Gi/o: lowers cAMP, opens K⁺ channels; on indirect-pathway neurons it releases the brake, and on dopamine neurons themselves it is the autoreceptor.
items.note: Its short isoform is the autoreceptor, the long one the postsynaptic receptor. Thick in the striatum and the pituitary.

items.name: Dopamine D3
items.binds: Dopamine, with the highest affinity of the five.
items.drugs: Pramipexole and ropinirole (Parkinson's, restless legs) prefer it. Cariprazine, the antipsychotic, is a partial agonist here.
items.effect: Gi/o signalling, like D2.
items.note: Confined to the limbic striatum: nucleus accumbens, islands of Calleja. Studied in addiction and in restless legs.

items.name: Dopamine D4
items.binds: Dopamine, moderate affinity; clozapine binds it well.
items.drugs: Clozapine binds it well. No drug aims at it alone.
items.effect: Gi/o signalling.
items.note: Sparse, in prefrontal cortex and the retina; a variable repeat in its gene was long linked to novelty seeking.

items.name: Dopamine D5
items.binds: Dopamine, with ten times the affinity of D1.
items.drugs: None.
items.effect: Gs: raises cAMP.
items.note: Rare: hippocampus, hypothalamus, and the cholinergic interneurons of the striatum.

groups.name: Adrenergic receptors
groups.note: Nine receptors for noradrenaline and adrenaline: α1 excites through Gq, α2 damps through Gi, β raises cAMP through Gs.

items.name: α1A
items.binds: Noradrenaline and adrenaline about equally, moderate affinity; prazosin blocks all three α1 receptors.
items.drugs: Prazosin and doxazosin (blood pressure; prazosin for PTSD nightmares), tamsulosin (prostate) block it. Phenylephrine, the decongestant, and midodrine switch it on. Many antipsychotics and antidepressants block it by accident: the dizziness on standing.
items.effect: Gq: Ca²⁺ release and PKC; a slow excitation of the cell.
items.note: Smooth muscle and, in the brain, the cortex and spinal motor neurons, where noradrenaline sharpens responsiveness.

items.name: α1B
items.binds: Noradrenaline and adrenaline, moderate affinity.
items.drugs: The same drugs as α1A: prazosin, doxazosin, phenylephrine.
items.effect: Gq signalling.
items.note: Blood vessels and the brain; the α1 receptor behind much of noradrenaline's arousal effect.

items.name: α1D
items.binds: Noradrenaline and adrenaline, moderate affinity.
items.drugs: The same drugs as α1A; tamsulosin touches it.
items.effect: Gq signalling.
items.note: Arteries and the cortex; the least studied of the three.

items.name: α2A
items.binds: Noradrenaline with high affinity; clonidine and guanfacine are its agonists.
items.drugs: Clonidine (blood pressure, ADHD, opioid withdrawal), guanfacine (ADHD), dexmedetomidine (sedation in intensive care) and tizanidine switch it on. Mirtazapine, the antidepressant, blocks it, which is how it raises noradrenaline and serotonin. Yohimbine.
items.effect: Gi/o: on noradrenergic terminals the autoreceptor that limits release; on prefrontal dendrites it closes HCN channels and strengthens working memory.
items.note: The receptor guanfacine works through in ADHD, and clonidine in opioid withdrawal.

items.name: α2B
items.binds: Noradrenaline and adrenaline, high affinity.
items.drugs: Clonidine and the other α2 agonists; mirtazapine blocks it.
items.effect: Gi/o signalling; in blood vessels it constricts.
items.note: Mostly peripheral; in the brain, the thalamus.

items.name: α2C
items.binds: Noradrenaline and adrenaline, high affinity.
items.drugs: Clonidine; mirtazapine blocks it.
items.effect: Gi/o signalling; a second autoreceptor, and a brake on dopamine release in the striatum.
items.note: Basal ganglia and hippocampus.

items.name: β1
items.binds: Noradrenaline and adrenaline with equal, moderate affinity; the beta-blockers' main target.
items.drugs: The beta-blockers: metoprolol, atenolol, bisoprolol, propranolol. Dobutamine switches it on in a failing heart.
items.effect: Gs: raises cAMP. In the heart, faster and stronger beats; in the brain, more cAMP in the cortex and hippocampus.
items.note: Cardiac muscle first, then the cortex and the pineal gland.

items.name: β2
items.binds: Adrenaline with much higher affinity than noradrenaline: this is the receptor the adrenal medulla's hormone reaches. Salbutamol is its agonist.
items.drugs: Salbutamol (Ventolin, albuterol), salmeterol and formoterol inhalers switch it on; adrenaline in an EpiPen. Propranolol blocks it: stage fright, migraine, and the softening of emotional memories.
items.effect: Gs: raises cAMP; relaxes bronchial and vascular smooth muscle. In the amygdala and hippocampus it strengthens emotional memories, which is what propranolol interrupts.
items.note: Lungs, blood vessels, astrocytes and the limbic system.

items.name: β3
items.binds: Noradrenaline over adrenaline, low affinity.
items.drugs: Mirabegron and vibegron (overactive bladder).
items.effect: Gs: raises cAMP; drives fat burning and relaxes the bladder.
items.note: Brown and white fat, bladder; little in the brain.

groups.name: Serotonin receptors
groups.note: Fourteen receptors, more than for any other transmitter. All but one are G-protein-coupled; 5-HT3 is a channel.

items.name: 5-HT1A
items.binds: Serotonin, high affinity; buspirone is a partial agonist, and many antipsychotics touch it.
items.drugs: Buspirone (anxiety) is a partial agonist; so are aripiprazole, vilazodone and vortioxetine in part. Every SSRI reaches it by raising serotonin. LSD and psilocin bind it as well as 5-HT2A.
items.effect: Gi/o: opens GIRK K⁺ channels, hyperpolarising. On raphe neurons the autoreceptor that limits their firing; on cortical and hippocampal pyramidal cells a brake on excitability.
items.note: The receptor behind the delay before SSRIs work: their effect waits for the raphe autoreceptors to desensitise.

items.name: 5-HT1B
items.binds: Serotonin, high affinity; triptans are its agonists.
items.drugs: The triptans: sumatriptan, rizatriptan, zolmitriptan (migraine). Ergotamine.
items.effect: Gi/o: on serotonin terminals the autoreceptor for release; on other terminals a brake on GABA and glutamate release. Constricts cranial blood vessels.
items.note: The migraine receptor, in the basal ganglia and on cerebral arteries.

items.name: 5-HT1D
items.binds: Serotonin and the triptans, high affinity.
items.drugs: The triptans and ergotamine.
items.effect: Gi/o: cuts release from trigeminal terminals.
items.note: Sparse; the other triptan receptor.

items.name: 5-HT1E
items.binds: Serotonin, low affinity; no selective drug.
items.drugs: None.
items.effect: Gi/o: lowers cAMP.
items.note: Cortex and hippocampus, in humans and few other species; its role is unknown.

items.name: 5-HT1F
items.binds: Serotonin, moderate affinity; lasmiditan is its selective agonist.
items.drugs: Lasmiditan (Reyvow), the migraine drug that does not narrow blood vessels.
items.effect: Gi/o: silences trigeminal terminals without constricting vessels.
items.note: The newest migraine target.

items.name: 5-HT2A
items.binds: Serotonin, moderate affinity; LSD, psilocin and mescaline are agonists here, and their potency as hallucinogens tracks their 5-HT2A affinity. Most atypical antipsychotics block it.
items.drugs: The classic psychedelics: LSD, psilocybin (as psilocin), mescaline, DMT, 2C-B. The atypical antipsychotics block it: clozapine, quetiapine, risperidone, olanzapine. Trazodone and mirtazapine block it, which helps sleep. Pimavanserin (Parkinson's psychosis).
items.effect: Gq: Ca²⁺ and PKC; a slow excitation of layer V pyramidal cells in the cortex.
items.note: Dense in the prefrontal cortex; the psychedelic receptor.

items.name: 5-HT2B
items.binds: Serotonin, high affinity; fenfluramine and ergot derivatives are agonists.
items.drugs: Fenfluramine (the diet drug withdrawn for heart-valve damage), pergolide and cabergoline at high dose, MDMA.
items.effect: Gq: proliferation and contraction in the heart valves and gut.
items.note: The reason fenfluramine and pergolide were withdrawn: valvular disease. Little in the brain.

items.name: 5-HT2C
items.binds: Serotonin, high affinity; lorcaserin was its agonist. Its mRNA is edited, giving receptors of different sensitivity.
items.drugs: Lorcaserin (the diet drug, withdrawn), agomelatine and mirtazapine block it; olanzapine too, part of the appetite. Fluoxetine touches it.
items.effect: Gq: excites GABA interneurons and so damps dopamine release; cuts appetite through the hypothalamus.
items.note: Choroid plexus, hypothalamus, striatum.

items.name: 5-HT3
items.binds: Serotonin, with micromolar affinity, at the interfaces of a pentamer; ondansetron and other setrons block it.
items.drugs: Ondansetron (Zofran), granisetron and palonosetron, the anti-sickness drugs of chemotherapy. Mirtazapine and vortioxetine block it. Alcohol potentiates it; metoclopramide blocks it weakly.
items.effect: A fast cation current, the only one serotonin produces directly. Excites interneurons in the cortex and the vagal afferents that trigger vomiting.
items.note: The anti-emetic receptor; the setrons act on it in the gut, the area postrema and the vagus.

items.name: 5-HT4
items.binds: Serotonin, high affinity; prucalopride is its agonist.
items.drugs: Prucalopride (constipation), metoclopramide in part; cisapride, withdrawn for heart rhythm.
items.effect: Gs: raises cAMP; speeds gut motility and boosts acetylcholine release in the hippocampus.
items.note: Gut, hippocampus, striatum.

items.name: 5-HT5A
items.binds: Serotonin, moderate affinity; no selective drug.
items.drugs: None.
items.effect: Gi/o: lowers cAMP.
items.note: Cortex, hippocampus, cerebellum; function uncertain.

items.name: 5-HT6
items.binds: Serotonin, high affinity; many antipsychotics and antidepressants block it.
items.drugs: No drug aims at it; clozapine, olanzapine and several antidepressants block it in passing.
items.effect: Gs: raises cAMP; modulates acetylcholine and glutamate release.
items.note: Confined to the brain: striatum, cortex, hippocampus. Antagonists were tried for cognition in Alzheimer's.

items.name: 5-HT7
items.binds: Serotonin, high affinity; blocked by some antipsychotics and by amisulpride.
items.drugs: No drug aims at it; aripiprazole, lurasidone and amisulpride touch it.
items.effect: Gs: raises cAMP; resets the circadian clock in the suprachiasmatic nucleus.
items.note: Thalamus, hypothalamus, hippocampus.

groups.name: Histamine receptors
groups.note: Four G-protein-coupled receptors, one of them the reason old antihistamines sedate.

items.name: Histamine H1
items.binds: Histamine, moderate affinity; diphenhydramine and the other first-generation antihistamines block it and cross into the brain.
items.drugs: The old antihistamines: diphenhydramine (Benadryl, Nytol), chlorphenamine, promethazine, hydroxyzine, and the sleep aids and cold remedies built on them. The non-drowsy ones, cetirizine and loratadine, which stay out of the brain. Doxepin at low dose (insomnia). Blocked by olanzapine, quetiapine and mirtazapine: the sedation and the weight gain.
items.effect: Gq: excites, closing K⁺ channels; in the cortex it keeps the cell awake.
items.note: Widespread; the receptor that makes antihistamines drowsy and antipsychotics fattening.

items.name: Histamine H2
items.binds: Histamine, moderate affinity; ranitidine and famotidine block it.
items.drugs: Famotidine (Pepcid), cimetidine, nizatidine; ranitidine (Zantac) until it was withdrawn.
items.effect: Gs: raises cAMP; drives acid secretion in the stomach and damps the after-hyperpolarisation in cortical neurons.
items.note: Stomach first, then basal ganglia and cortex.

items.name: Histamine H3
items.binds: Histamine with the highest affinity of the four; pitolisant is an inverse agonist.
items.drugs: Pitolisant (Wakix) for narcolepsy blocks it, raising histamine and wakefulness.
items.effect: Gi/o: the autoreceptor on histamine terminals, and a brake on release of acetylcholine, dopamine, noradrenaline and serotonin.
items.note: The wake-promoting target: blocking it raises histamine and treats narcolepsy.

items.name: Histamine H4
items.binds: Histamine, high affinity.
items.drugs: None in everyday use.
items.effect: Gi/o: chemotaxis of immune cells.
items.note: Mast cells, eosinophils, microglia; barely in neurons.

groups.name: Purine receptors
groups.note: Adenosine's four G-protein-coupled receptors, and ATP's seven channels and eight G-protein-coupled receptors.

items.name: Adenosine A1
items.binds: Adenosine, high affinity, enough to sense the level that builds through waking. Caffeine and theophylline block it.
items.drugs: Caffeine and theophylline block it: tea, coffee, energy drinks. Adenosine itself, injected, resets a racing heart through it.
items.effect: Gi/o: opens K⁺ channels and closes Ca²⁺ channels, cutting release of glutamate. The brain's general brake.
items.note: Everywhere, thickest in cortex, hippocampus and cerebellum. The receptor sleep pressure works through.

items.name: Adenosine A2A
items.binds: Adenosine, high affinity; caffeine blocks it, and istradefylline is a selective antagonist.
items.drugs: Caffeine blocks it; istradefylline (Nourianz) blocks it for Parkinson's. Regadenoson (heart scans) switches it on.
items.effect: Gs: raises cAMP. In the striatum it sits with D2, opposing it; in the ventrolateral preoptic area it promotes sleep.
items.note: Concentrated in the striatum; the other caffeine receptor, and a Parkinson's target.

items.name: Adenosine A2B
items.binds: Adenosine, low affinity: only the concentrations of injury or hypoxia reach it.
items.drugs: Caffeine, weakly.
items.effect: Gs: raises cAMP; in astrocytes and mast cells.
items.note: Glia and vasculature more than neurons.

items.name: Adenosine A3
items.binds: Adenosine, low affinity in humans.
items.drugs: None in everyday use.
items.effect: Gi/o signalling; anti-inflammatory.
items.note: Immune cells, and little in the brain.

items.name: P2X1
items.binds: ATP, high affinity; desensitises within a second.
items.drugs: None.
items.effect: A fast cation current.
items.note: Smooth muscle and platelets more than neurons.

items.name: P2X2
items.binds: ATP, moderate affinity, slow to desensitise.
items.drugs: None.
items.effect: Sustained cation current; on sensory and autonomic neurons and in the cochlea.
items.note: Often paired with P2X3 in taste and pain afferents.

items.name: P2X3
items.binds: ATP, high affinity, fast to desensitise; gefapixant blocks it.
items.drugs: Gefapixant (chronic cough) blocks it.
items.effect: Fast cation current on sensory nerve endings.
items.note: The ATP receptor of pain, bladder sensation and the cough reflex.

items.name: P2X4
items.binds: ATP, moderate affinity; ivermectin potentiates it.
items.drugs: Ivermectin potentiates it in passing.
items.effect: Cation current with high Ca²⁺ permeability; in microglia it triggers release of BDNF.
items.note: The microglial receptor behind neuropathic pain.

items.name: P2X5
items.binds: ATP, moderate affinity; most humans carry a non-functional splice variant.
items.drugs: None.
items.effect: Small cation current.
items.note: Little known.

items.name: P2X6
items.binds: ATP; will not assemble on its own and appears only in mixed receptors.
items.drugs: None.
items.effect: Modest cation current, in combination.
items.note: Cerebellum and hippocampus, with P2X2 or P2X4.

items.name: P2X7
items.binds: ATP with the lowest affinity of the family: it needs the hundreds of micromolar that only damaged cells leak.
items.drugs: None approved; blockers have been tried for depression and arthritis.
items.effect: A cation channel that, held open, dilates into a large pore and starts inflammation, releasing interleukin-1β.
items.note: Microglia and astrocytes; the damage sensor.

items.name: P2Y1
items.binds: ADP over ATP, high affinity.
items.drugs: None.
items.effect: Gq: Ca²⁺ release; in astrocytes the main route of calcium waves.
items.note: Astrocytes, platelets, and neurons of the cortex and cerebellum.

items.name: P2Y2
items.binds: ATP and UTP equally, moderate affinity.
items.drugs: Diquafosol (dry eye, in Japan).
items.effect: Gq: Ca²⁺ release; drives secretion in epithelia.
items.note: Epithelia, glia, endothelium.

items.name: P2Y4
items.binds: UTP, with ATP as an antagonist in humans.
items.drugs: None.
items.effect: Gq signalling.
items.note: Gut epithelium, choroid plexus.

items.name: P2Y6
items.binds: UDP, high affinity, over other nucleotides.
items.drugs: None.
items.effect: Gq: in microglia it triggers phagocytosis of dying cells.
items.note: Microglia: the 'eat me' receptor.

items.name: P2Y11
items.binds: ATP, low affinity; absent in rodents.
items.drugs: None.
items.effect: Gs and Gq both: raises cAMP and Ca²⁺.
items.note: Immune cells and the spleen; rarely in the brain.

items.name: P2Y12
items.binds: ADP, high affinity; clopidogrel and ticagrelor block it.
items.drugs: The blood thinners clopidogrel (Plavix), ticagrelor and prasugrel block it.
items.effect: Gi/o: lowers cAMP. In platelets it drives aggregation; in microglia it is the receptor that sends processes towards injury within minutes.
items.note: Platelets and microglia, where it is the marker of the resting, surveying state.

items.name: P2Y13
items.binds: ADP, high affinity.
items.drugs: None.
items.effect: Gi/o signalling.
items.note: Spleen, and sparsely in the brain.

items.name: P2Y14
items.binds: UDP-glucose and UDP, moderate affinity.
items.drugs: None.
items.effect: Gi/o signalling; a damage sensor on immune cells.
items.note: Glia and immune cells.

groups.name: Cannabinoid receptors
groups.note: Two G-protein-coupled receptors for the brain's own lipid messengers, and for THC.

items.name: CB1
items.binds: 2-AG as a full agonist and anandamide as a partial one, both with high affinity; THC is a partial agonist. Sits on the presynaptic terminal, facing the cell that made the endocannabinoid.
items.drugs: THC, the active part of cannabis, and its prescribed forms dronabinol and nabilone; nabiximols (Sativex). The synthetic cannabinoids sold as spice or K2, which are full agonists and far more dangerous. CBD acts on it only indirectly. Rimonabant blocked it and was withdrawn for depression.
items.effect: Gi/o: closes Ca²⁺ channels and opens K⁺ channels on the terminal, so release drops. The retrograde brake on both GABA and glutamate synapses.
items.note: The most abundant GPCR in the brain: basal ganglia, cerebellum, hippocampus, cortex. Rimonabant blocked it and was withdrawn for depression.

items.name: CB2
items.binds: 2-AG and anandamide, high affinity.
items.drugs: THC weakly; CBD indirectly. No selective drug in use.
items.effect: Gi/o signalling; damps inflammation.
items.note: Microglia and immune cells; rises in the brain with injury and inflammation.

groups.name: Opioid receptors
groups.note: Four G-protein-coupled receptors for the endogenous opioid peptides, three of which morphine and its relatives act on.

items.name: μ-opioid receptor (MOR)
items.plain: Mu opioid receptor, the morphine receptor
items.binds: β-endorphin and the enkephalins with high affinity, endomorphins too; morphine, fentanyl, oxycodone and methadone are agonists, naloxone the antagonist.
items.drugs: Morphine, heroin, fentanyl, oxycodone, hydrocodone, codeine, methadone, tramadol; buprenorphine, the partial agonist; loperamide (Imodium), which stays in the gut. Naloxone (Narcan) and naltrexone block it. Kratom's mitragynine acts here.
items.effect: Gi/o: opens K⁺ channels and closes Ca²⁺ channels. In the periaqueductal grey it silences the GABA cells that hold pain control back; in the ventral tegmental area the same trick frees dopamine release.
items.note: The receptor of opioid analgesia, euphoria, constipation and respiratory depression, all of it.

items.name: δ-opioid receptor (DOR)
items.binds: The enkephalins with high affinity, β-endorphin less so; no approved drug is selective for it.
items.drugs: No selective drug in use; buprenorphine and methadone touch it.
items.effect: Gi/o signalling; analgesia with less euphoria, and an antidepressant tone in animals.
items.note: Cortex, striatum, olfactory bulb.

items.name: κ-opioid receptor (KOR)
items.binds: The dynorphins with high affinity; salvinorin A is a potent agonist.
items.drugs: Salvinorin A, from Salvia divinorum, the most potent natural hallucinogen. Pentazocine and nalbuphine. Naltrexone and buprenorphine block it; a blocker, aticaprant, is in trials for depression.
items.effect: Gi/o: cuts dopamine release in the nucleus accumbens. Dysphoria rather than euphoria.
items.note: Hypothalamus, striatum, spinal cord; the receptor of stress-induced aversion.

items.name: Nociceptin receptor (NOP)
items.binds: Nociceptin/orphanin FQ with high affinity; insensitive to naloxone and to morphine.
items.drugs: None in use; buprenorphine is a partial agonist here. Cebranopadol in trials.
items.effect: Gi/o signalling; blocks stress analgesia and damps reward.
items.note: Cortex, amygdala, hypothalamus; the fourth member, found from its receptor's sequence before its ligand was known.

groups.name: Neuropeptide receptors
groups.note: All G-protein-coupled, and answering to peptides that are released only when a neuron fires hard. A selection of the best known.

items.name: NK1 (substance P)
items.binds: Substance P with the highest affinity, neurokinin A and B less; aprepitant blocks it.
items.drugs: Aprepitant (Emend) and fosaprepitant block it for chemotherapy nausea.
items.effect: Gq: slow excitation. On dorsal horn neurons it carries persistent pain; in the brainstem it triggers vomiting.
items.note: Dorsal horn, striatum, amygdala; the anti-emetic aprepitant's target.

items.name: NK2 (neurokinin A)
items.binds: Neurokinin A over substance P.
items.drugs: None in everyday use.
items.effect: Gq: smooth muscle contraction.
items.note: Gut and airways more than brain.

items.name: NK3 (neurokinin B)
items.binds: Neurokinin B, high affinity; fezolinetant blocks it.
items.drugs: Fezolinetant (Veozah) blocks it for hot flushes.
items.effect: Gq signalling; drives the kisspeptin neurons that pulse GnRH.
items.note: Hypothalamus; the receptor fezolinetant blocks to treat hot flushes.

items.name: NPY Y1
items.binds: Neuropeptide Y and peptide YY with high affinity.
items.drugs: None.
items.effect: Gi/o: damps excitability; in the hypothalamus it drives feeding, in the amygdala it lowers anxiety.
items.note: Cortex, hypothalamus, amygdala.

items.name: NPY Y2
items.binds: Neuropeptide Y and PYY(3–36), the gut's satiety form, with high affinity.
items.drugs: None.
items.effect: Gi/o: presynaptic, cutting release of NPY, glutamate and GABA; in the arcuate nucleus it suppresses appetite.
items.note: Hippocampus, hypothalamus; the receptor PYY(3–36) reaches after a meal.

items.name: NPY Y4
items.binds: Pancreatic polypeptide over NPY.
items.drugs: None.
items.effect: Gi/o signalling; slows gastric emptying.
items.note: Brainstem and hypothalamus.

items.name: NPY Y5
items.binds: Neuropeptide Y, high affinity.
items.drugs: None; blockers were tried for obesity.
items.effect: Gi/o signalling; with Y1, the feeding receptor.
items.note: Hypothalamus and hippocampus.

items.name: Somatostatin SSTR1
items.binds: Somatostatin-14 and -28, high affinity.
items.drugs: None.
items.effect: Gi/o: lowers cAMP, opens K⁺ channels.
items.note: Cortex and hippocampus.

items.name: Somatostatin SSTR2
items.binds: Somatostatin, high affinity; octreotide binds it best.
items.drugs: Octreotide and lanreotide (acromegaly, gut tumours).
items.effect: Gi/o: inhibits hormone release and dendritic excitability.
items.note: Pituitary, cortex, and the receptor octreotide works through against acromegaly.

items.name: Somatostatin SSTR3
items.binds: Somatostatin, high affinity.
items.drugs: None.
items.effect: Gi/o signalling; in the primary cilium of neurons.
items.note: Cerebellum, cortex.

items.name: Somatostatin SSTR4
items.binds: Somatostatin, high affinity.
items.drugs: None.
items.effect: Gi/o signalling; analgesic and anti-inflammatory in animals.
items.note: Hippocampus and cortex.

items.name: Somatostatin SSTR5
items.binds: Somatostatin-28 over -14; pasireotide binds it.
items.drugs: Pasireotide (Cushing's disease).
items.effect: Gi/o: inhibits growth hormone and insulin release.
items.note: Pituitary, hypothalamus.

items.name: Orexin OX1
items.binds: Orexin-A with high affinity, orexin-B less; suvorexant blocks both orexin receptors.
items.drugs: Suvorexant (Belsomra), lemborexant and daridorexant, the orexin sleeping pills, block it.
items.effect: Gq: slow excitation of the locus coeruleus and the ventral tegmental area.
items.note: The arousal receptor: its loss, or its ligand's, is narcolepsy.

items.name: Orexin OX2
items.binds: Orexin-A and orexin-B equally, high affinity.
items.drugs: The same three sleeping pills.
items.effect: Gq: excites the histamine neurons of the tuberomammillary nucleus.
items.note: The receptor whose mutation causes canine narcolepsy; daridorexant's target for insomnia.

items.name: Oxytocin receptor
items.binds: Oxytocin with high affinity, vasopressin with lower.
items.drugs: Oxytocin (Pitocin, Syntocinon) to start labour; carbetocin. Atosiban blocks it to delay labour.
items.effect: Gq: excites; in the amygdala and nucleus accumbens it tunes social approach, in the uterus it contracts.
items.note: Hypothalamus, amygdala, nucleus accumbens, uterus.

items.name: Vasopressin V1a
items.binds: Vasopressin, high affinity, oxytocin lower.
items.drugs: None in everyday use.
items.effect: Gq: constricts vessels; in the brain shapes social memory and, in voles, pair bonding.
items.note: Blood vessels, lateral septum, ventral pallidum.

items.name: Vasopressin V1b
items.binds: Vasopressin, high affinity.
items.drugs: None in everyday use.
items.effect: Gq: in the pituitary drives ACTH release with CRF.
items.note: Pituitary and hippocampus; a stress-axis receptor.

items.name: CRF1
items.binds: Corticotropin-releasing factor with high affinity, urocortin-1 too.
items.drugs: None approved; blockers were tried for depression and anxiety and failed.
items.effect: Gs: raises cAMP. In the pituitary it releases ACTH; in the amygdala and locus coeruleus it drives the anxiety of stress.
items.note: The receptor that starts the stress response.

items.name: CRF2
items.binds: The urocortins with high affinity, CRF itself with less.
items.drugs: None.
items.effect: Gs signalling; in the raphe and the septum it tends to calm rather than alarm.
items.note: Septum, raphe, hypothalamus; the counterweight to CRF1.

items.name: Melanocortin MC4
items.binds: α-MSH as agonist; agouti-related peptide is its natural antagonist, and setmelanotide a drug agonist.
items.drugs: Setmelanotide (Imcivree) for genetic obesity; bremelanotide (Vyleesi) for low sexual desire.
items.effect: Gs: raises cAMP in the paraventricular nucleus, suppressing appetite.
items.note: Hypothalamus; the commonest single-gene cause of severe obesity when mutated.

items.name: Melatonin MT1
items.binds: Melatonin with picomolar affinity, the highest of any receptor on this page; ramelteon and agomelatine are agonists.
items.drugs: Melatonin itself, sold over the counter; ramelteon (Rozerem); agomelatine, the antidepressant; tasimelteon.
items.effect: Gi/o: quietens the suprachiasmatic nucleus at night and constricts cerebral arteries.
items.note: Suprachiasmatic nucleus, pituitary.

items.name: Melatonin MT2
items.binds: Melatonin, high affinity.
items.drugs: The same: melatonin, ramelteon, agomelatine, tasimelteon.
items.effect: Gi/o: shifts the phase of the circadian clock.
items.note: Suprachiasmatic nucleus, retina, hippocampus.

items.name: Prostaglandin EP1
items.binds: Prostaglandin E₂, moderate affinity.
items.drugs: Aspirin, ibuprofen, naproxen and diclofenac act one step up, stopping the prostaglandin being made; paracetamol probably does the same in the brain.
items.effect: Gq: Ca²⁺ release; sensitises pain fibres.
items.note: Kidney, and sparsely in the brain.

items.name: Prostaglandin EP2
items.binds: Prostaglandin E₂, low affinity.
items.drugs: The same NSAIDs, upstream.
items.effect: Gs: raises cAMP; in microglia it amplifies inflammation.
items.note: Cortex, hippocampus, microglia.

items.name: Prostaglandin EP3
items.binds: Prostaglandin E₂ with the highest affinity of the four.
items.drugs: The NSAIDs upstream, which is how they bring a fever down. Misoprostol switches it on.
items.effect: Gi/o: in the preoptic area it is the receptor through which fever is set, which is what aspirin stops upstream.
items.note: The fever receptor, in the median preoptic nucleus.

items.name: Prostaglandin EP4
items.binds: Prostaglandin E₂, high affinity.
items.drugs: The NSAIDs upstream; indometacin closes a baby's ductus arteriosus through it.
items.effect: Gs: raises cAMP; anti-inflammatory in microglia, and keeps the ductus arteriosus open before birth.
items.note: Widespread, including the hippocampus.

items.name: Bradykinin B1
items.binds: des-Arg⁹-bradykinin, the breakdown product, high affinity; hardly expressed until injury induces it.
items.drugs: None in everyday use.
items.effect: Gq signalling; chronic pain and inflammation.
items.note: Induced in inflamed tissue and injured nerve.

items.name: Bradykinin B2
items.binds: Bradykinin, high affinity; icatibant blocks it.
items.drugs: Icatibant blocks it (hereditary angioedema). ACE inhibitors raise bradykinin, hence their cough.
items.effect: Gq: Ca²⁺ release and prostaglandin synthesis; the receptor of the sharp pain of injury.
items.note: Sensory nerve endings, blood vessels; icatibant's target in angioedema.

groups.name: TRP channels
groups.note: Cation channels of the senses: opened by temperature, chemicals and stretch as much as by any ligand.

items.name: TRPV1
items.plain: Transient receptor potential vanilloid 1, the chilli receptor
items.binds: Capsaicin with high affinity, heat above about 43 °C, protons, and anandamide; each lowers the threshold for the others.
items.drugs: Capsaicin, in chillies and in capsaicin creams and the Qutenza patch. Paracetamol's breakdown product AM404 acts here and at TRPA1 in the spinal cord, which may be part of how it works.
items.effect: A Ca²⁺-rich cation current that fires the pain fibre. Held open, it desensitises the fibre, which is how capsaicin cream works.
items.note: The heat and chilli receptor, on C fibres and in the hypothalamus.

items.name: TRPM8
items.plain: Transient receptor potential melastatin 8, the menthol receptor
items.binds: Menthol and icilin, and cold below about 26 °C.
items.drugs: Menthol, in Vicks, cough sweets and cooling gels. Eucalyptol.
items.effect: Cation current on cold-sensing fibres.
items.note: The cold and menthol receptor.

items.name: TRPA1
items.plain: Transient receptor potential ankyrin 1, the mustard receptor
items.binds: Allyl isothiocyanate (mustard oil), acrolein, and the electrophiles of smoke and tear gas, by covalent attachment.
items.drugs: Mustard oil, wasabi, horseradish, cinnamon, the sting of onions and tear gas. Paracetamol's metabolite AM404. Gas anaesthetics irritate through it.
items.effect: Cation current on nociceptors and vagal afferents; cough, tears and the sting of wasabi.
items.note: The chemical-irritant receptor, alongside TRPV1 on the same fibres.

items.name: TRPM3
items.binds: Pregnenolone sulfate and noxious heat.
items.drugs: None in use.
items.effect: Cation current on sensory neurons; part of heat pain with TRPV1 and TRPA1.
items.note: Sensory ganglia; mutations cause epilepsy.

groups.name: Voltage-gated channels
groups.note: Not receptors, and nothing binds them, but every receptor on this page acts through them: the sodium and potassium channels of the action potential and the calcium channels of release.

items.name: Nav1.1
items.binds: Nothing: it opens on depolarisation past about −55 mV and inactivates within a millisecond. Tetrodotoxin blocks it in the nanomolar range.
items.drugs: Local anaesthetics: lidocaine, bupivacaine, and cocaine's numbing. Phenytoin, carbamazepine, lamotrigine (epilepsy) slow it. Tetrodotoxin, the pufferfish poison, blocks it.
items.effect: The rising phase of the action potential in fast-spiking GABA interneurons.
items.note: Its loss in interneurons is Dravet syndrome: a sodium channel mutation that causes epilepsy by silencing inhibition.

items.name: Nav1.2
items.binds: Voltage; tetrodotoxin-sensitive.
items.drugs: The same local anaesthetics and epilepsy drugs; tetrodotoxin.
items.effect: Action potentials in unmyelinated axons and the immature initial segment.
items.note: Cortex and hippocampus early in life; mutations cause epilepsy and autism.

items.name: Nav1.6
items.binds: Voltage; tetrodotoxin-sensitive, and carries a persistent and a resurgent current as well as the transient one.
items.drugs: The same local anaesthetics and epilepsy drugs; riluzole (motor neuron disease) damps its persistent current.
items.effect: The channel of the adult initial segment and of every node of Ranvier: where the spike starts and how it jumps.
items.note: Clustered by ankyrin-G at the initial segment; the channel drawn at the nodes on the plates above.

items.name: Nav1.7
items.binds: Voltage, with a threshold near rest that amplifies small depolarisations.
items.drugs: Local anaesthetics; no selective drug has yet succeeded.
items.effect: Sets the threshold of pain fibres.
items.note: People born without it feel no pain; gain-of-function mutations cause erythromelalgia. A much-pursued analgesic target.

items.name: Nav1.8
items.binds: Voltage; tetrodotoxin-resistant, and works at potentials where other sodium channels have inactivated.
items.drugs: Suzetrigine (Journavx), approved in 2025, the first non-opioid painkiller that blocks a single sodium channel. Local anaesthetics.
items.effect: The upstroke of the action potential in C-fibre nociceptors.
items.note: Confined to sensory neurons; another pain target.

items.name: Cav1.2 (L-type)
items.binds: Voltage, opening at strong depolarisation; dihydropyridines such as nifedipine block it.
items.drugs: The blood-pressure drugs amlodipine, nifedipine, felodipine, verapamil and diltiazem block it.
items.effect: A long-lasting Ca²⁺ current on the cell body and dendrites that drives gene expression, and in the heart the plateau of every beat.
items.note: Heart, smooth muscle, and neuronal dendrites; variants are linked to bipolar disorder.

items.name: Cav1.3 (L-type)
items.binds: Voltage, opening at lower potentials than Cav1.2.
items.drugs: The same calcium-channel blockers, weakly; isradipine was tried for Parkinson's.
items.effect: Pacemaking in the sinoatrial node and in dopamine neurons, whose slow Ca²⁺ load may be why they are lost in Parkinson's disease.
items.note: Cochlear hair cells, heart, substantia nigra.

items.name: Cav2.1 (P/Q-type)
items.binds: Voltage; ω-agatoxin blocks it.
items.drugs: Gabapentin and pregabalin bind its α2δ partner and quieten it. No direct blocker in use.
items.effect: The Ca²⁺ that triggers transmitter release at most central synapses and at the neuromuscular junction.
items.note: Presynaptic terminals; mutations cause familial hemiplegic migraine and ataxia.

items.name: Cav2.2 (N-type)
items.binds: Voltage; ω-conotoxin from cone snails blocks it, as does ziconotide, its drug form. Gi/o-coupled receptors close it directly.
items.drugs: Ziconotide (Prialt), the cone-snail toxin given into the spine for severe pain. Gabapentin and pregabalin through α2δ. Opioids and cannabinoids close it indirectly.
items.effect: Release at sympathetic and sensory terminals, including the pain synapses of the dorsal horn.
items.note: The channel opioids and cannabinoids close to stop release.

items.name: Cav2.3 (R-type)
items.binds: Voltage; resistant to the toxins that block the others.
items.drugs: None.
items.effect: A residual Ca²⁺ current in dendritic spines and some terminals.
items.note: Hippocampus and cerebellum.

items.name: Cav3 (T-type)
items.binds: Voltage, opening near rest and inactivating fast: a transient, low-threshold current. Ethosuximide blocks it.
items.drugs: Ethosuximide (absence seizures), zonisamide; mibefradil, withdrawn.
items.effect: Bursts. When a thalamic neuron is hyperpolarised these channels recover, and the next small depolarisation fires a burst of spikes on top of a Ca²⁺ spike.
items.note: Thalamus; the rhythm of sleep spindles and of absence seizures, which ethosuximide treats.

items.name: Kv1 (delayed rectifier)
items.binds: Voltage; dendrotoxin from mamba venom blocks it, and 4-aminopyridine.
items.drugs: Dalfampridine (4-aminopyridine) blocks it to speed walking in multiple sclerosis.
items.effect: Repolarises the action potential and sets the threshold at the initial segment and the juxtaparanodes.
items.note: Axons; 4-aminopyridine's target in multiple sclerosis.

items.name: Kv2.1
items.binds: Voltage, opening slowly at strong depolarisation.
items.drugs: None.
items.effect: The delayed rectifier of the cell body: keeps repetitive firing going without depolarisation block.
items.note: Somatic clusters on cortical and hippocampal neurons.

items.name: Kv4 (A-type)
items.binds: Voltage, opening and inactivating quickly at sub-threshold potentials.
items.drugs: None.
items.effect: A transient outward current that delays the first spike and damps back-propagating action potentials in dendrites.
items.note: Dendrites of pyramidal cells; the current that lets a neuron fire slowly.

items.name: Kv7 (M-current, KCNQ)
items.binds: Voltage, at rest: a slow, non-inactivating current. Muscarinic M1 receptors close it, which is how it was named; retigabine opens it.
items.drugs: Retigabine opened it for epilepsy and was withdrawn; azetukalner is in trials. Flupirtine.
items.effect: Sets the resting potential and stops repetitive firing.
items.note: Initial segment and nodes; mutations cause neonatal epilepsy.

items.name: Kv11.1 (hERG)
items.binds: Voltage, with fast inactivation and slow recovery; blocked by many drugs by accident.
items.drugs: Blocked on purpose by sotalol, dofetilide and amiodarone (heart rhythm), and by accident by erythromycin, haloperidol, methadone, citalopram and dozens more: the QT-prolongation warning on the label.
items.effect: Repolarises the heart's action potential.
items.note: Heart, and some neurons; the reason every new drug is tested for QT prolongation.

items.name: HCN1
items.binds: Voltage, but backwards: opens on hyperpolarisation, and cAMP opens it a little more. Ivabradine blocks the family.
items.drugs: Ivabradine blocks the family; gabapentin and propofol touch it.
items.effect: The h-current: a cation current that pulls a hyperpolarised cell back towards threshold, and in distal dendrites damps the summation of inputs.
items.note: Dendrites of cortical and hippocampal pyramidal cells.

items.name: HCN2
items.binds: Hyperpolarisation, and strongly cAMP: this is the isoform noradrenaline speeds up.
items.drugs: Ivabradine (heart rate); lamotrigine touches it.
items.effect: Pacemaking in the thalamus and the heart's sinoatrial node.
items.note: Thalamus, heart, and the pain fibres where it drives neuropathic firing.

groups.name: Background and Ca²⁺-activated K⁺ channels
groups.note: The channels that set how a neuron rests and how it recovers from firing.

items.name: BK (KCa1.1)
items.binds: Ca²⁺ arriving inside, and depolarisation together; iberiotoxin blocks it.
items.drugs: None in use.
items.effect: A large K⁺ current that sharpens the action potential and cuts release at the terminal.
items.note: Presynaptic terminals, the cell body, and smooth muscle.

items.name: SK (KCa2)
items.binds: Ca²⁺ inside, through calmodulin, at sub-micromolar levels; apamin from bee venom blocks it.
items.drugs: None in use; apamin from bee venom blocks it.
items.effect: The medium after-hyperpolarisation that follows a burst and sets the firing rate.
items.note: Dendritic spines, where it damps NMDA currents, and dopamine neurons, where it sets their pacemaker rhythm.

items.name: Kir2 (inward rectifier)
items.binds: Nothing outside; the channel is open at rest and blocked from inside by Mg²⁺ and polyamines when the cell depolarises.
items.drugs: None in use; chloroquine blocks it in passing.
items.effect: Holds the resting potential near the K⁺ equilibrium and lets go once the cell fires.
items.note: Muscle, heart and neurons; mutations cause Andersen–Tawil syndrome.

items.name: GIRK (Kir3)
items.binds: The βγ subunits of Gi/o proteins, from inside: GABA-B, D2, μ-opioid, 5-HT1A, A1, M2 and α2 receptors all open it.
items.drugs: Opened indirectly by opioids, baclofen, clonidine and every Gi-coupled drug; alcohol opens it directly, part of the sedation.
items.effect: A slow K⁺ current that hyperpolarises the cell for hundreds of milliseconds: the common effector of inhibitory metabotropic receptors.
items.note: Dendrites throughout the brain; the channel drawn under 'K⁺ open' in the GPCR schematics above.

items.name: K-ATP (Kir6)
items.binds: ATP from inside closes it; ADP opens it. Sulfonylureas close it, diazoxide opens it.
items.drugs: The diabetes drugs gliclazide and glibenclamide close it; diazoxide, minoxidil (Rogaine) and nicorandil open it.
items.effect: Couples metabolism to excitability: when energy runs low the channel opens and the cell falls quiet.
items.note: Pancreatic β cells, where it controls insulin, and hypothalamic glucose sensors.

items.name: TREK-1 (K2P2)
items.binds: Membrane stretch, heat, polyunsaturated fatty acids and volatile anaesthetics open it; Gq and Gs receptor signalling close it.
items.drugs: The gas anaesthetics isoflurane and sevoflurane open it; riluzole and fluoxetine touch it.
items.effect: A background K⁺ leak that sets the resting potential; opening it is part of how anaesthetics quieten neurons.
items.note: Cortex, hippocampus, sensory neurons.

items.name: TASK-1 and TASK-3 (K2P3, K2P9)
items.plain: Two-pore-domain potassium leak channels TASK-1 and TASK-3
items.binds: Closed by extracellular acid, opened by anaesthetics; muscarinic and other Gq receptors close them.
items.drugs: Opened by the gas anaesthetics; blocked by acid.
items.effect: Leak K⁺ current that keeps motor neurons and cerebellar granule cells at rest; closing it is the excitation acetylcholine gives.
items.note: Motor neurons, cerebellum, carotid body.

groups.name: Transporters
groups.note: Not receptors, but they bind the transmitters more selectively than many receptors do: the reuptake carriers that end a signal, and the vesicular carriers that load the next.

items.name: EAAT2 (GLT-1)
items.binds: Glutamate, with micromolar affinity, three Na⁺ and one H⁺ carried in, one K⁺ out. Aspartate as well.
items.drugs: None in use; ceftriaxone raises its levels in research.
items.effect: Clears most of the glutamate released in the brain, within milliseconds, into astrocytes. Its loss is excitotoxic.
items.note: Astrocyte membranes facing the synapse; ninety per cent of glutamate uptake.

items.name: EAAT1 (GLAST)
items.binds: Glutamate and aspartate, micromolar affinity, Na⁺-coupled.
items.drugs: None.
items.effect: Glutamate clearance in the cerebellum and retina.
items.note: Bergmann glia and Müller cells.

items.name: EAAT3 (EAAC1)
items.binds: Glutamate and cysteine, Na⁺-coupled.
items.drugs: None.
items.effect: Neuronal uptake, and the cysteine supply for glutathione.
items.note: Neuronal dendrites; a minor route for glutamate itself.

items.name: GAT-1
items.binds: GABA, micromolar affinity, with two Na⁺ and one Cl⁻; tiagabine blocks it.
items.drugs: Tiagabine (epilepsy) blocks it.
items.effect: Reuptake of GABA into the terminal that released it, ending inhibition.
items.note: GABA terminals and astrocytes; tiagabine's target in epilepsy.

items.name: GlyT1
items.binds: Glycine, with two Na⁺ and one Cl⁻.
items.drugs: None approved; bitopertin and iclepertin have been tried for schizophrenia.
items.effect: Clears glycine from around NMDA receptors, so it sets how much co-agonist they see; blocking it boosts NMDA currents.
items.note: Astrocytes and glutamatergic neurons in the forebrain.

items.name: GlyT2
items.binds: Glycine, with three Na⁺ and one Cl⁻: the extra sodium lets it fill the terminal to high concentration.
items.drugs: None.
items.effect: Reloads inhibitory terminals with glycine for the next release.
items.note: Glycinergic terminals of the spinal cord and brainstem; mutations cause hyperekplexia.

items.name: Dopamine transporter (DAT)
items.binds: Dopamine with sub-micromolar affinity, Na⁺- and Cl⁻-coupled; cocaine and methylphenidate block it, amphetamine runs it backwards.
items.drugs: Cocaine, methylphenidate (Ritalin, Concerta) and modafinil block it; amphetamine (Adderall), methamphetamine and MDMA reverse it. Bupropion blocks it weakly.
items.effect: Ends the dopamine signal by taking it back into the terminal. Where it is sparse, as in the prefrontal cortex, the noradrenaline transporter does the job instead.
items.note: Dopamine terminals in the striatum; its loss on a DaT scan is the imaging sign of Parkinson's disease.

items.name: Noradrenaline transporter (NET)
items.binds: Noradrenaline, and dopamine almost as well; atomoxetine, reboxetine and the tricyclics block it, amphetamine reverses it.
items.drugs: Atomoxetine (Strattera) and reboxetine block it, as do the SNRIs venlafaxine and duloxetine, the tricyclics, bupropion, cocaine and methylphenidate; amphetamine reverses it.
items.effect: Reuptake of noradrenaline, and of prefrontal dopamine.
items.note: Noradrenergic terminals; atomoxetine's target in ADHD.

items.name: Serotonin transporter (SERT)
items.binds: Serotonin, with nanomolar affinity; every SSRI binds it, and MDMA reverses it.
items.drugs: The SSRIs fluoxetine (Prozac), sertraline (Zoloft), citalopram, escitalopram, paroxetine; the SNRIs; the tricyclics; tramadol; MDMA (ecstasy), which reverses it. St John's wort in part.
items.effect: Ends the serotonin signal; blocking it raises synaptic serotonin within hours, though the antidepressant effect waits weeks.
items.note: Serotonin terminals and platelets; the target of fluoxetine, sertraline and the rest.

items.name: VMAT2
items.binds: Dopamine, noradrenaline, serotonin and histamine, in exchange for two H⁺ from the vesicle's acid interior; reserpine and tetrabenazine block it.
items.drugs: Reserpine, tetrabenazine, deutetrabenazine and valbenazine (Huntington's chorea, tardive dyskinesia) block it; amphetamine and methamphetamine disrupt it.
items.effect: Loads monoamines into vesicles. Blocked, the terminals empty and the transmitter is destroyed by monoamine oxidase.
items.note: Monoamine vesicles; tetrabenazine's target in Huntington's chorea.

items.name: VGLUT1 and VGLUT2
items.binds: Glutamate, low affinity, driven by the vesicle's membrane potential; aspartate is refused.
items.drugs: None.
items.effect: Fills vesicles with glutamate, which is what makes a terminal glutamatergic.
items.note: VGLUT1 in cortex and hippocampus, VGLUT2 in thalamus and brainstem.

items.name: VGAT (VIAAT)
items.binds: GABA and glycine both, driven by the vesicle's proton gradient.
items.drugs: None.
items.effect: Fills inhibitory vesicles; one carrier for both inhibitory transmitters.
items.note: GABA and glycine terminals.

items.name: VAChT
items.binds: Acetylcholine, exchanged for two H⁺; vesamicol blocks it.
items.drugs: None in use; vesamicol in the laboratory.
items.effect: Loads acetylcholine into vesicles at the neuromuscular junction and in the brain.
items.note: Cholinergic terminals; the PET marker of cholinergic loss in dementia.
